summary: Gives guidelines for how 6Bone sites should operate, so the 6Bone could stay a quality experimentation environment. It defines accepted best practice for configuring interior and exterior routing protocols there. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 2772.

eli5.summary: The 6Bone was a practice playground for the new internet addresses. This sets house rules for the people running it so nothing breaks.

subtitle: Guidelines for operating the IPv6 testbed network.

tldr.problem: The 6Bone, an IPv6 experimental network, suffered from routing problems when sites advertised incorrect routes, breaking the testbed's quality as a research environment.
tldr.mechanism: This document establishes best practices for both interior (RIPng) and exterior (BGP4+) routing protocols, defining which routes should and should not be advertised and how to aggregate them.
tldr.outcome: By following these guidelines, 6Bone sites can prevent routing failures and maintain a stable testbed for IPv6 experimentation. The 6Bone itself was replaced by RFC 2772 with updated practices.

today: RFC 2772 replaced this document with updated 6Bone operational guidelines.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The 6Bone is an experimental network for testing IPv6 protocols and products before they are deployed widely. As the network grew, sites began advertising routes incorrectly (called "bogus routes"), causing packets to be misrouted or dropped. This document defines best current practice for configuring routing protocols on the 6Bone, covering both Interior Gateway Protocols (IGPs) like RIPng and Exterior Gateway Protocols (EGPs) like BGP4+.

The 6Bone is organized in a hierarchy: pseudo Top Level Aggregators (pTLAs) form a backbone, pseudo Next Level Aggregators (pNLAs) provide transit, and leaf sites are the end users. The backbone routers use BGP4+ to exchange routing information among each other.
sections.eli5: When a clubhouse network got too big, some people were giving wrong directions, so the leaders wrote down rules about which directions (routes) everyone could announce.

sections.title: Hierarchical Structure and Mandatory Protocols
sections.content:
The 6Bone uses a three-tier structure designed to support IPv6 address aggregation. At the core, pTLA routers form a mesh and MUST use BGP4+ as the mandatory routing protocol. Multi-homed sites and pNLAs SHOULD also use BGP4+ to ensure they can advertise their routes correctly to upstream providers. Regular leaf sites MAY use a simple default route to their ISP.

Each level has different responsibilities: pTLA sites must maintain the backbone, pNLAs provide regional transit service, and leaf sites connect through a pNLA or pTLA.
sections.eli5: The network had three levels: top managers (pTLAs) at the center, regional managers (pNLAs) in between, and local offices (leaf sites) at the edges. Each level had to talk to the next one in a certain way.

sections.title: Special Address Prefixes and What Not to Advertise
sections.content:
Certain IPv6 address ranges are reserved for special purposes and MUST NOT be advertised in any routing protocol. Link-local prefixes (FE80::/10) have scope limited to a single link and make no sense to route. Site-local prefixes (FEC0::/10) are internal to a site and MUST NOT leave it. Loopback (::1/128) and unspecified addresses (::0/128) are never routable. Multicast prefixes must not be in unicast routing tables, and IPv4-compatible (::a.b.c.d) and IPv4-mapped (::FFFF:a.b.c.d) addresses have strict limits on where they can be advertised.

Additionally, undefined unicast prefixes from outside the 2000::/3 range, including RFC 2471 test addresses, MUST NOT appear in the 6Bone.
sections.eli5: Some addresses are only for talking to neighbors (link-local), some are only for a single site (site-local), and some are for special purposes like multicasting. You can't announce these on the 6Bone because they don't make sense to route.

sections.title: Route Aggregation and Prefix Management
sections.content:
Every border router MUST perform route aggregation to keep routing tables small. Sites and pNLAs MUST only advertise to their upstream provider the prefixes assigned by that ISP, and MUST NOT advertise prefixes more specific than /48 (the granularity of ISP allocations). pTLAs MUST NOT advertise prefixes longer than /24 to each other unless special peering agreements are in place, and must take care not to leak more specific routes to pTLAs outside those agreements.

Inter-site links connecting the backbone MUST use global IPv6 addresses, not IPv4-compatible tunnels, and the link prefixes themselves MUST NOT be injected into global routing tables.
sections.eli5: When announcing routes, everybody had to combine smaller routes into bigger ones to keep the routing tables clean. Sites could only announce the addresses they were actually given, not anything more specific.

sections.title: The 6Bone Registry and Enforcement
sections.content:
Each 6Bone site MUST maintain entries in the 6Bone registry (a RIPE-181 database with IPv6 extensions), including IPv6-site descriptions, prefix delegations (Inet6num), and maintainer contacts (Mntner). The registry is at whois.6bone.net and serves as the authoritative source for finding ISPs and understanding site relationships.

Enforcement was voluntary but expected: pTLA sites commit to the rules when they join, and are responsible for enforcing them among sites they allocate addresses to. When a site detects a problem, it first contacts the site maintainer using the registry. If that fails, the issue goes to the 6Bone Operations group (defined by the 6bone@isi.edu mailing list) for coordination. For product issues, sites contact vendors directly.
sections.eli5: Every site had to be listed in a public phone book (the registry) so others could find their contacts and understand who was who. If someone broke the rules, other sites would first try talking to them, then ask the 6Bone leaders for help.
